What slows healthcare teams down

We begin with the moments where people wait, repeat work, or lose context. Then we automate the predictable part and keep judgment with the right person.

  • Phones and WhatsApp overwhelm the front desk

    Booking calls, report requests, insurance questions and directions all land on the same few lines and personal phones. Patients wait on hold, messages sit unanswered after hours, and staff retype details into the HIS by hand.

  • Missed appointments and idle slots

    Patients forget, cannot get through to reschedule, or arrive unprepared for a test or procedure. Slots go unused while other patients wait, and consultants' days start late or run over.

  • Reports and discharge papers are hard to get

    Families chase lab reports and discharge summaries by phone or in person. Forwarded PDFs travel without access control, and nobody can show who received what, or when.

  • Insurance paperwork slows admission and discharge

    Cashless pre-authorization depends on complete documents from the family, the treating doctor and billing. A missing policy card or an unanswered insurer query keeps patients waiting at the discharge desk.

  • Clinical safety cannot be left to a chatbot

    Patients describe symptoms in chat and expect advice. Any automation has to recognize clinical and emergency messages and hand them to qualified staff at once, never answer them itself.

  • Patient data rules are tightening

    The DPDP Act and Rules set duties for notice, consent, security safeguards, logs and breach handling that phase in by mid-2027. ABDM, drug rules and messaging platform policies add conditions of their own, and patient details kept in spreadsheets and on staff phones are hard to secure, log or erase on request.

One consented WhatsApp front door, from booking to follow-up

One WhatsApp Business number, linked to your HIS and used only with patients who opt in, handles booking, reminders, rescheduling, arrival updates and follow-up. Routine requests complete automatically. Symptoms, medicine questions and complaints go to a staffed queue, and emergency words get an immediate instruction to call the hospital's emergency line or 112. Every message is logged against the patient's consent.

What changes

  • Fewer missed appointments, because confirming or rescheduling takes a single tap
  • Faster first responses to routine requests, including after hours
  • Front-desk time shifts from routine bookings to patients who need a person
  • Clinical questions reliably reach qualified staff, with an audit trail of every handoff
  1. 1

    Capture consent and purpose

    Patients opt in at registration, on the website or by scanning a QR code at reception, and choose the message types they want. The consent record, notice version and channel are stored, and replying STOP to any message withdraws consent.

    WBWhatsApp Business PlatformSSupabase
  2. 2

    Book against live HIS slots

    A WhatsApp Flow offers department, doctor, date and slot from the HIS scheduling API and writes the booking back; where the HIS has no API, a synced slot table holds it for the front desk to confirm. The confirmation carries preparation notes the department wrote.

    WBWhatsApp Business Platformnn8n
  3. 3

    Route free text safely

    Every message is screened for emergency words and phrases in the languages the hospital serves, then a model sorts it into booking, billing, directions, report request, symptom or complaint. Only administrative intents are answered, from approved content; everything else opens a ticket in the staffed queue.

    ACAnthropic Claudenn8nRRetool
  4. 4

    Remind and reschedule in one tap

    Approved reminder templates go out at intervals the hospital sets, with confirm, reschedule and cancel buttons. Released slots return to the HIS and are offered to waitlisted patients with an approved template.

    WBWhatsApp Business Platformnn8n
  5. 5

    Update on arrival and after the visit

    On arrival the patient receives a token and queue position updates. After the visit, the follow-up the doctor recorded in the HIS and a short feedback request are scheduled automatically.

    WBWhatsApp Business Platformnn8nSSupabase
  6. 6

    Watch the queue and the numbers

    Operations leads see unanswered conversations, failed messages, no-shows and response times by department, and can open any individual case for service recovery.

    RRetoolMPMicrosoft Power BISSentry

  7. People decide

    Patient-relations agents own the live queue in agreed hours, and a duty nurse or doctor takes every symptom or medicine message. The medical superintendent and the hospital's legal or compliance owner approve templates, emergency wording and routing rules before launch and after every change.

Walk through the patient journey

A clear delivery rhythm

Five phases with named deliverables, client inputs, and review points. Most teams start with a focused pilot.

  1. 1

    1–2 weeks

    Discover

    We walk the patient journey with front office, nursing, lab and pharmacy staff, on site or by video, map where calls and delays pile up, and review what the HIS, LIS or POS can expose. We also review current consent forms, the privacy notice and existing messaging practices.

  2. 2

    1–2 weeks

    Design

    We design conversation flows, templates, routing rules and data flows, including the emergency and symptom handling script. Clinical content and consent wording are written or approved by your team, not by us.

  3. 3

    2–4 weeks

    Build

    We build the integrations in n8n and the agreed tools against a test environment with synthetic or de-identified data, set up the consent log, staff queues and dashboards, and document every connection and credential owner.

  4. 4

    1–2 weeks

    Validate & launch

    We test with front-office staff, nurses and pharmacists, run a scripted set of symptom, emergency and edge-case messages, fix what fails and launch in one department, unit or branch before any wider rollout.

  5. 5

    Ongoing, with monthly reviews

    Operate & improve

    We monitor failed messages, template quality ratings, handoffs and model accuracy, review KPIs with your owners each month, and change content and rules only through a controlled, approved change process.

First pilot: Five-week OPD booking and reminder pilot

Start with one OPD department or doctor group. The first two weeks connect its slots, get templates approved and run the safety script; for three live weeks patients book, confirm and reschedule on WhatsApp while every symptom or complaint reaches a staffed queue. We compare no-shows and response times with the weeks before, using your own HIS data.

  • One OPD department or doctor group on the hospital's verified WhatsApp Business number
  • Booking, confirmation, reminder and reschedule templates approved by Meta and your clinical lead
  • Emergency and symptom routing to a named, staffed queue during agreed hours
  • Consent log and a daily report of failed or unanswered messages
  • Baseline and pilot comparison of no-shows and first response time

Know whether it is working

Proposed measures, agreed with your team before launch, with a source, owner, and review cadence.

Appointment no-show rate
Share of booked appointments in a period where the patient neither attended nor canceled or rescheduled before the slot, measured from HIS records.
First response time on patient messages
Elapsed time from an inbound patient message to the first meaningful reply by automation or staff, reported separately for staffed and unstaffed hours.
Arrival-to-consultation wait
Median time from token issue or registration to the start of consultation, by department and hour, from HIS or token system timestamps.
Report turnaround time
Time from sample receipt or scan completion to an authorized report available to the patient, by test category.
